proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(\beta\in\mathcal K\), and abbreviate
\[
\mathcal A_{\beta}
=\mathfrak R_{\beta}(\mathfrak M)\cap\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}.
\]
By the definition of intersection, \(\mathcal A_{\beta}\subseteq
\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}\).  It remains to prove that the inclusion is
proper.  We do so with one deterministic triangular-array witness.

Let \(a\in\mathbb R^p\) be a unit vector, let
\(e_1,\ldots,e_p\) be the standard basis, and put
\(L_n=\lfloor(n-1)/(2p)\rfloor\).  Construct
\(\widetilde x_{1n},\ldots,\widetilde x_{nn}\) by setting
\(\widetilde x_{1n}=0\), using \(L_n\) copies of each pair
\((e_j,-e_j)\), \(1\le j\le p\), among the remaining rows, and setting
all unused rows equal to zero.  Thus
\[
\max_{i\le n}\lVert\widetilde x_{in}\rVert\le1,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde x_{in}=0,
\qquad
\widetilde S_{xx,n}
:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
\widetilde x_{in}\widetilde x_{in}^{\mathsf T}
=\frac{2L_n}{n-1}I_p
\longrightarrow \frac1p I_p=:\Sigma.
\]
In particular, \(\Sigma\in\mathbb S_{++}^p\).  For every admissible
\(n\), define
\[
x_{1n}^{\star}=n^{1/4}a,
\qquad
x_{in}^{\star}=\widetilde x_{in}\quad(2\le i\le n),
\qquad
Y_{in}^{\star}(q)=a^{\mathsf T}x_{in}^{\star}
\quad(q\in\mathcal Q).
\]
Since the unperturbed rows sum to zero and
\(\widetilde x_{1n}=0\), the new mean is
\(\bar x_n^{\star}=n^{-3/4}a\).  The finite-population covariance is
therefore exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx,n}^{\star}
&:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n
(x_{in}^{\star}-\bar x_n^{\star})
(x_{in}^{\star}-\bar x_n^{\star})^{\mathsf T}\\
&=\frac1{n-1}\left{
\sum_{i=1}^n x_{in}^{\star}(x_{in}^{\star})^{\mathsf T}
-n\bar x_n^{\star}\bar x_n^{\star\mathsf T}\right}\\
&=\widetilde S_{xx,n}
+\frac{n^{1/2}-n^{-1/2}}{n-1}aa^{\mathsf T}
\longrightarrow\Sigma.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the limiting baseline covariance is nonsingular, as required by
the covariance part of the definition of \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}\).

We next verify the outcome covariance clauses of that definition.  The
outcome is the same function of the baseline under every treatment, so,
for all \(q,q'\in\mathcal Q\),
\[
\bar Y_n^{\star}(q)=a^{\mathsf T}\bar x_n^{\star}\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
S_{qq',n}^{\star}=a^{\mathsf T}S_{xx,n}^{\star}a
\longrightarrow a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a,
\qquad
S_{q,x,n}^{\star}=a^{\mathsf T}S_{xx,n}^{\star}.
\]
The nonconstant Walsh columns satisfy
\(\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}c_q=0\).  Consequently every unit-level
factorial-effect vector vanishes:
\[
2^{1-K_f}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}c_qY_{in}^{\star}(q)
=2^{1-K_f}\left(\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}c_q\right)
a^{\mathsf T}x_{in}^{\star}=0.
\]
Thus its finite-population covariance is identically zero and, in
particular, converges.

For completeness, the positive-definiteness clause for the projected
factorial covariance can be checked directly.  Let
\(\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{x,n}\) stack the \(F\) factorial contrasts
of the balanced treatment-group baseline means.  Under balanced complete
randomization, direct inclusion-indicator algebra gives, for treatment
combinations \(q,q'\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sqrt n\,\bar x_n(q),
\sqrt n\,\bar x_n(q')\right)
=\begin{cases}
(Q-1)S_{xx,n}^{\star},&q=q',\\
-S_{xx,n}^{\star},&q\ne q'.
\end{cases}
\]
Indeed, each group has size \(n/Q\), so the diagonal covariance is
\(n\{Q/n-1/n\}S_{xx,n}^{\star}\), while two distinct group means have
covariance \(-S_{xx,n}^{\star}/n\) before multiplication by \(n\).
Using \(2^{1-K_f}=2/Q\),
\(\mathbf C^{\mathsf T}\mathbf 1_Q=0\), and
\(\mathbf C^{\mathsf T}\mathbf C=QI_F\), the preceding display yields
\[
V_{xx,n}^{\star}
:=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sqrt n\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{x,n}\right)
=4(I_F\otimes S_{xx,n}^{\star}).
\]
Moreover, the equality
\(Y_{in}^{\star}(q)=a^{\mathsf T}x_{in}^{\star}\) implies the exact
estimator identity
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}_n^{\star}
=(I_F\otimes a^{\mathsf T})
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{x,n}.
\]
The outcome estimator is therefore entirely in the linear span of the
covariate-imbalance estimator.  Its projected covariance, in the same
root-\(n\) normalization, is
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_{\tau\tau,n}^{\parallel,\star}
&=(I_F\otimes a^{\mathsf T})V_{xx,n}^{\star}
(I_F\otimes a)\\
&=4(a^{\mathsf T}S_{xx,n}^{\star}a)I_F
\longrightarrow4(a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma a)I_F
\in\mathbb S_{++}^{F},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last inclusion uses \(a\ne0\) and
\(\Sigma\in\mathbb S_{++}^p\).

Finally, the maximum-negligibility clauses hold because the ordinary rows
are bounded and the sole exceptional row has norm \(n^{1/4}\):
\[
\frac1n\max_{i\le n}
\lVert x_{in}^{\star}-\bar x_n^{\star}\rVert^2
=O(n^{-1/2})\longrightarrow0,
\]
and, since \(\lVert a\rVert=1\),
\[
\frac1n\max_{i\le n,\,q\in\mathcal Q}
\left|Y_{in}^{\star}(q)-\bar Y_n^{\star}(q)\right|^2
\le
\frac1n\max_{i\le n}
\lVert x_{in}^{\star}-\bar x_n^{\star}\rVert^2
\longrightarrow0.
\]
The covariance limits, positive projected limit, and the two negligible-
maximum limits are precisely the deterministic-array requirements in the
definition of \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}\) (with its allocation-share
restriction excluded).  Hence the constructed array belongs to
\(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}\).

On the other hand,
\[
\sup_n\max_{i\le n}\lVert x_{in}^{\star}\rVert
\ge\sup_n\lVert x_{1n}^{\star}\rVert
=\sup_n n^{1/4}=\infty.
\]
This contradicts \(\mathrm{ass{:}baseline\text{-}bound}\), which is a
member condition of \(\mathfrak M\) by \(\mathrm{def{:}model\text{-}class}\).
Because the baseline array is deterministic, every probability-one
realization class \(\mathfrak R_{\beta}(\mathfrak M)\) inherits that
bound.  The witness therefore does not belong to
\(\mathfrak R_{\beta}(\mathfrak M)\), while it does belong to
\(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}\).  It follows that
\[
\mathfrak R_{\beta}(\mathfrak M)\cap\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}
\subsetneq\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{HD}}.
\]
The witness is independent of \(\beta\), so the conclusion holds for
every \(\beta\in\mathcal K\).

Write \(\mu_{q,\beta}(x)=E_{\beta}\{Y(q)\mid X=x\}\) and \(v_{q,\beta}(x)=E_{\beta}\{Y(q)^2\mid X=x\}\).  For \(0\leq j\leq3\), let \(\mathscr F_j\) be the finite collection consisting of all scalar coordinates of the functions needed to form the assignment covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}_{\beta}\{\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(0),\Delta_T\}\) and the imbalance covariance \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_T)\), after applying \(D_{\rho}^{j}\).  Direct expansion of the two finite sums defining \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(0)\) and \(\Delta_T\) shows that these functions are finite products and linear combinations of coordinates of \(x\), \(xx^{\mathsf T}\), \(D_{\rho}^{\ell}\mu_{q,\beta}(x)\), and \(D_{\rho}^{\ell}v_{q,\beta}(x)\), where \(q\in\mathcal Q\) and \(0\leq\ell\leq j\).  The exact coefficients are the balanced-assignment probabilities
\[
 P(Z_i=q)=\frac1Q,
 \qquad
 P(Z_i=q,Z_j=q)=\frac{k-Q}{Q^2(k-1)},
 \qquad
 P(Z_i=q,Z_j=q')=\frac{k}{Q^2(k-1)}quad(q\ne q',\ i\ne j).
 \tag{1}
\]
Thus no distributional approximation is used in this reduction.

By \(\mathrm{ass{:}arraywise\text{-}moment\text{-}regularity}\), every member of every \(\mathscr F_j\) is jointly continuous and uniformly bounded on the common compact set \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal K\).  Joint continuity on a compact set gives uniform equicontinuity in \(\beta\).  If \(\nu_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_{in}}\), then \(\mathrm{ass{:}baseline\text{-}limit}\) gives, for every fixed \(\beta\), convergence of the integral of each such function under \(\nu_n\) to its integral under \(\nu\).  A finite \(\beta\)-net and uniform equicontinuity therefore yield
\[
 \max_{0\leq j\leq3}\ \max_{f\in\mathscr F_j}
 \sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
 \left|\int f(x,\beta)\,\nu_n(dx)-\int f(x,\beta)\,\nu(dx)\right|\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{2}
\]
This is the standard finite-net proof: for a net point use weak convergence, and for an arbitrary \(\beta\) bound the two off-net differences by the common modulus of continuity.

For any split \(S\) of size \(m\), put \(T=S^c\), so \(|T|=N\).  For a function bounded in absolute value by \(C\), the identity
\[
 \frac1N\sum_{i\in T}f(x_{in},\beta)-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(x_{in},\beta)
 =\frac mN\left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(x_{in},\beta)-\frac1m\sum_{i\in S}f(x_{in},\beta)\right\}
\]
implies
\[
 \sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
 \left|\frac1N\sum_{i\in T}f(x_{in},\beta)-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nf(x_{in},\beta)\right|
 \leq \frac{2Cm}{N}=o(1).
 \tag{3}
\]
The same bound applies to all members of all \(\mathscr F_j\).  Hence (2)--(3) give a common limit, uniformly through three \(\rho\)-derivatives, for every empirical moment entering the full-array and complement oracle constructions.  The complement convergence is in fact uniform over all splits, and therefore implies the asserted convergence in \(P_{S_m}\)-probability.

We next propagate these moment limits through the two matrix operations in \(\mathcal B_T\).  Let \(S_T=|T|^{-1}\sum_{i\in T}(x_{in}-\bar x_T)(x_{in}-\bar x_T)^{\mathsf T}\).  Expanding \(\Delta_T\) and using (1) and the Walsh identities \(\sum_qc_q=0\) and \(\mathbf C^{\mathsf T}\mathbf C=QI_F\), one obtains
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(\Delta_T)=\frac4{k-1}\,(I_F\otimes S_T).
 \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, \(\Delta_T=(2/k)\sum_{i\in T}c_{Z_i}\otimes(x_{in}-\bar x_T)\), while \(E(c_{Z_i}c_{Z_i}^{\mathsf T})=I_F\) and \(E(c_{Z_i}c_{Z_j}^{\mathsf T})=-I_F/(k-1)\) for \(i\ne j\).  The same expansion (1) shows that \((k-1)\operatorname{Cov}_{\beta}\{\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(0),\Delta_T\}/4\) is a finite linear combination of the empirical moments already controlled in (2)--(3).  Multiplying both covariance factors in the definition of \(\mathcal B_T\) by \((k-1)/4\) does not change their product.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}baseline\text{-}gram}\), the eigenvalues of \(S_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}\) are bounded away from zero and infinity.  Equation (3), applied to the first two baseline moments, gives the same bounds for every complement once \(m/n\to0\).  Consequently the Moore--Penrose inverse in \(\mathcal B_T\), after this common scaling, is an ordinary inverse on the relevant range, and inversion is uniformly smooth there.  Differentiating the identity \(AA^{-1}=I\),
\[
 D(A^{-1})[H]=-A^{-1}HA^{-1},
 \tag{5}
\]
and iterating (5) through order three proves that the covariance limit from (2)--(3) propagates uniformly through \(\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_T)^{+}\).  It follows that there is a \(C^3\) matrix map \(\mathcal B_{\infty}(\beta)\) satisfying
\[
 \max_{0\leq j\leq3}\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
 \left\|D_{\rho}^{j}\mathcal B_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)-D_{\rho}^{j}\mathcal B_{\infty}(\beta)\right\|\to0
 \tag{6}
\]
and the identical conclusion for \(T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}\), uniformly over the split.

Set \(M_T(\beta)=\mathcal B_T(\beta)^{\mathsf T}W\mathcal B_T(\beta)\) and \(M_{\infty}(\beta)=\mathcal B_{\infty}(\beta)^{\mathsf T}W\mathcal B_{\infty}(\beta)\).  Since \(W\in\mathbb S_{++}^{F}\), these matrices are positive semidefinite, and (6) plus the product rule gives
\[
 \max_{0\leq j\leq3}\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}
 \left\|D_{\rho}^{j}M_T(\beta)-D_{\rho}^{j}M_{\infty}(\beta)\right\|\to0
 \tag{7}
\]
along both experiment-indexed sequences.  On the constant positive-rank stratum imposed by \(\mathrm{ass{:}oracle\text{-}rank}\), \(M_{\infty}(\beta)\ne0\).  Continuity and compactness therefore give
\[
 \inf_{\beta\in\mathcal K}\operatorname{tr}M_{\infty}(\beta)>0.
 \tag{8}
\]
By (7)--(8), the trace denominator is also uniformly positive for the two finite-array sequences for all sufficiently large \(n\).  The quotient rule through order three now applies uniformly to
\[
 G_T(\beta)=\mathcal N\{M_T(\beta)\}
 =\frac{M_T(\beta)}{\operatorname{tr}M_T(\beta)}.
\]
Defining
\[
 G_{\infty}(\beta)=\frac{M_{\infty}(\beta)}{\operatorname{tr}M_{\infty}(\beta)}
\]
therefore proves both displayed convergences in the lemma, including all \(\rho\)-derivatives of orders zero through three.  Positivity, trace one, (8), and the quotient rule also show \(G_{\infty}\in C^3(\mathcal K;\mathbb S_+^{Fp})\), completing the proof.

Set \(d=Fp\).  By \(\mathrm{lem{:}experiment\text{-}indexed\text{-}oracle\text{-}convergence}\), every \(G_{\infty}(\beta)\) is a limit of nonzero trace-normalized oracle scores.  Hence it is positive semidefinite with trace one.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}oracle\text{-}rank}\), its rank is the fixed positive integer \(r_G\).  The max--min variational formulas for ordered eigenvalues show directly that they are continuous functions of a symmetric matrix in operator norm.  Continuity on compact \(\mathcal K\) and the constant-rank condition therefore give a number \(\lambda_->0\) such that every positive eigenvalue of every \(G_{\infty}(\beta)\) belongs to \([\lambda_-,1]\).

Rotational invariance of \(Z\) shows that
\[
 Z^{\mathsf T}G_{\infty}(\beta)Z
 \ \stackrel{d}{=}\ \sum_{j=1}^{r_G}\lambda_j(\beta)\xi_j^2,
\]
where the \(\xi_j\) are independent standard normal variables and the ordered positive eigenvalues \(\lambda_j(\beta)\) are continuous as an unordered multiset.  Convolution of the scaled chi-square densities shows that the right-hand side has a finite, continuous, strictly positive density at every \(u>0\).  The same convolution formula, dominated on compact subsets of \((0,\infty)\) by the bounds \(\lambda_j\in[\lambda_-,1]\), makes its distribution function and density jointly continuous in \((\beta,u)\).

The inequalities
\[
 \lambda_-\chi^2_{r_G}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{r_G}\lambda_j(\beta)\xi_j^2\leq\chi^2_{r_G}
\]
hold under the displayed coupling.  Since \(0<\alpha<1\), they place all \(q_{\alpha,\beta}\) in one compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\).  Joint continuity and strict monotonicity of the distribution functions then imply continuity of \(\beta\mapsto q_{\alpha,\beta}\).  Joint continuity and positivity of the density on the compact quantile graph give
\[
 0<\min_{\beta\in\mathcal K}f_\beta(q_{\alpha,\beta})
 \leq\max_{\beta\in\mathcal K}f_\beta(q_{\alpha,\beta})<\infty.
\]

For completeness, continuity of the coarea moments can be checked without selecting eigenvectors globally.  The spectral projection onto the range of \(G_{\infty}(\beta)\) is continuous because the spectrum is uniformly separated from zero.  On a neighborhood of any fixed \(\beta\), projecting a fixed basis and applying Gram--Schmidt supplies continuous orthonormal frames for the range and null space.  In these coordinates the positive range block \(A_\beta\) has eigenvalues in \([\lambda_-,1]\).  On the level set \(r^{\mathsf T}A_\beta r=u\), make the change of variables
\[
 r=\sqrt u\,A_\beta^{-1/2}\omega,
 \qquad \omega\in\mathbb S^{r_G-1}.
\]
After the null Gaussian coordinates are integrated out, each denominator, first moment, and second moment in the definition of \(\mathcal C\) is an integral over the fixed unit sphere of a polynomial in \(\omega\), \(D_{\rho_a}G_{\infty}(\beta)\), and \(D_{\rho_b}G_{\infty}(\beta)\), multiplied by a Gaussian factor and continuous determinant powers of \(A_\beta\).  On a compact neighborhood of the quantile graph these integrands have one common integrable bound because \(u\) is bounded away from zero and the eigenvalues are in \([\lambda_-,1]\).  Dominated convergence therefore gives continuity of all raw coarea moments.  The denominator equals the strictly positive density just treated, so taking ratios and subtracting products proves continuity of \(\mathcal C(\beta,u)\).

The defining formula for \(\Gamma\), together with continuity of \(f\), \(q\), and \(\mathcal C\), proves continuity of \(\Gamma\).  Finally, under the additional condition stated in the claim, inversion is continuous on \(\mathbb S_{++}^r\); compactness keeps the inverse bounded.  Composition with matrix multiplication and trace then proves continuity of \(B\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The already-declared arraywise moment condition must be part of model membership: without it, weak convergence of the empirical baseline law does not control conditional moments at off-support triangular-array points. This correction makes the model class agree with the regularity used by the experiment-indexed oracle convergence proof.

proposed.statement:
For every member of \(\mathfrak M\) there is a common \(G_{\infty}\in C^3(\mathcal K;\mathbb S_{+}^{Fp})\) such that, for every balanced \(m=m(n)\) with \(m\to\infty\), \(N\to\infty\), and \(m/n\to0\),
\[
\max_{0\le j\le3}\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}\lVert D_{\rho}^{j}G_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta)-D_{\rho}^{j}G_{\infty}(\beta)\rVert\to0,
\]
and
\[
\max_{0\le j\le3}\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal K}\lVert D_{\rho}^{j}G_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(\beta)-D_{\rho}^{j}G_{\infty}(\beta)\rVert\xrightarrow{P_{S_m}}0.
\]
Here \(D_{\rho}^{0}G=G\), the first display is deterministic conditional on the complete baseline array, and the second probability is over the uniform pilot split conditional on that array.
proposed.justification: The common experiment-indexed limit removes ambiguity about which empirical oracle and which convergence mode define the boundary constants.
proposed.gap: First-order learned-rerandomization arguments require consistency of one selected score, whereas the second-order boundary expansion needs uniform convergence of the oracle map and its first three quotient derivatives along both realized experiment sequences.
proposed.consumer: It gives replication planners one stable limiting geometry whether the oracle is evaluated on all registered units or on the random main-wave complement.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof directly uses arraywise moment regularity and the positive constant-rank stratum, so those assumptions must be declared in the target's dependency metadata after the model-class correction.

open_obligations.what_is_open: A uniform second-order one-wave oracle-gain or deletion-stability expansion strong enough to leave no term at the pilot-frontier scale.
open_obligations.obstruction: First-order finite-population Gaussian convergence gives only a little-oh remainder relative to one over the wave size. At the square-root pilot scale the theorem needs cancellation or a refined order-two expansion, including exact boundary ties and unequal Horvitz--Thompson inclusions; no frozen node supplies it.
open_obligations.attempted: Centered at the empirical oracle and Taylor-expanded the random-complement empirical moments. This closes the subset algebra conditional on an order-two one-wave expansion, but that finite-randomization expansion remains unproved.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The exact accounting theorem reduces this node to a one-wave expansion.  If one establishes, uniformly on regular subsets,
\[
d_T(\beta)=\frac{A(\beta,M_T)}{|T|}+O(|T|^{-2}),
\]
where \(M_T\) is the finite vector of empirical moments and \(A(\beta,\cdot)\) has two bounded derivatives, then uniform-subset identities give \(E(M_T-M_n)=0\) and \(E\lVert M_T-M_n\rVert^2=O\{m/(nN)\}\).  Taylor expansion then yields
\[
d_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}-\left(\frac Nn\right)^2E d_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}
=A(\beta,M_n)\frac{m}{n^2}+O\!\left(\frac{m}{n^3}+\frac1{n^2}\right),
\]
which has the required remainder on the interior pilot scale.  The missing part is the uniform finite-randomization expansion for \(d_T\).

open_obligations.what_is_open: The uniform local asymptotic minimax transfer from the adaptive pilot experiment to exact finite Horvitz--Thompson action loss for arbitrary measurable actions.
open_obligations.obstruction: Quadratic-mean differentiability and information regularity identify the candidate Gaussian shift, but they do not by themselves establish a uniformly efficient pilot estimator with quadratic-loss uniform integrability, localization of unrestricted actions, or the shrinking finite-boundary comparison.
open_obligations.attempted: Derived the outcome-only likelihood architecture and the Gaussian boundary Hessian. The remaining bridge is precisely the finite comparison plus uniform decision-theoretic localization, so assuming the trace constant would assume the theorem's crux.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The fixed-baseline and product-law assumptions imply that the pilot likelihood ratio contains only the \(m\) revealed conditional outcome likelihood ratios.  Under the stated quadratic-mean differentiability conditions its formal central sequence is
\[
\Delta_m=m^{-1/2}\sum_{i\in S_m}s_{Z_i,\beta}(Y_{in}(Z_i)\mid x_{in}),
\]
with nuisance-efficient information \(I_{\mathrm{eff}}\).  The proved Gaussian boundary calculation makes the candidate quadratic action loss equal to \(h^{\mathsf T}\Gamma(\beta)h\), so an efficient Gaussian shift would give \(\operatorname{tr}\{\Gamma I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}\}\).  What is not established is the uniform triangular-array LAN-to-decision transfer together with the exact finite Horvitz--Thompson boundary comparison for unrestricted measurable actions.

open_obligations.what_is_open: The uniform second-order expansion and its matching arbitrary-action lower bound.
open_obligations.obstruction: Exact accounting isolates exactly two terms, but both coefficient-level asymptotics are unresolved: the oracle deletion term and the exact finite learned-action regret. Treating either as a hypothesis would violate the anti-laundering requirement.
open_obligations.attempted: Proved the exact decomposition and inserted the proposed coefficient expansions algebraically. This confirms there is no additional cross-wave term, while showing that the desired theorem is equivalent to the two unresolved uniform comparisons.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The exact accounting theorem proves the algebraic reduction
\[
R_{n,m}-R_n^{\mathrm{or}}
=\left\{d_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}-\left(\frac Nn\right)^2E d_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}\right\}
+\left(\frac Nn\right)^2E\{V_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(\widehat G_m)-V_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}}(G_{T_{n,m}^{\mathrm{main}}})\}.
\]
Thus the advertised expansion follows immediately once the first bracket is shown to equal \(A(\beta)m/n^2+o\{m/n^2+(nm)^{-1}\}\) uniformly and the second to equal \(B(\beta)/(nm)+o\{m/n^2+(nm)^{-1}\}\) uniformly.  Those are precisely the two unresolved finite comparisons; the exact identity introduces no third term.

open_obligations.what_is_open: Uniform minimax lower bounds for bounded pilots, positive pilot fractions, and nonvanishing main-wave fractions outside the interior expansion.
open_obligations.obstruction: The corrected one-wave inequality is memberwise unless a common moment envelope is added, and the frozen results contain no first-order comparison showing that arbitrary finite actions cannot beat the raw Gaussian oracle over those endpoint windows.
open_obligations.attempted: Established the nearly-all-pilot argument conditional on a fixed-member moment envelope and positive full-oracle gain. The other windows require a two-point testing or first-order localization argument not present in the frozen core.
open_obligations.partial_result: For a fixed model member with a common conditional second-moment envelope, the corrected one-wave bound implies that the greatest possible contribution of a main wave of size \(N\) to the pooled risk is \(O(N/n^2)\).  Therefore, if the first-order full-oracle gain satisfies \(n d_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(\beta_0)\to A(\beta_0)>0\), every sequence with \(N=o(n)\) has excess at least \(A(\beta_0)/(2n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), and its \(n^{3/2}\)-scaled excess diverges.  Bounded-pilot and positive-fraction windows still require a first-order arbitrary-action lower comparison that is not supplied by the frozen assumptions.

open_obligations.what_is_open: The statistical transfer from the interior risk expansion and endpoint exclusions to the global minimax pilot sequence.
open_obligations.obstruction: The deterministic optimization is proved, but its premises are the still-open uniform second-order risk theorem and endpoint lemma. Therefore positivity of the finite minimax denominator and convergence of every near-minimizing pilot sequence cannot yet be concluded.
open_obligations.attempted: Proved uniqueness, the convex-hull formula, and the two-active-state certificate, and checked the subsequence argument conditional on coercive endpoint exclusion. No unconditional route bypasses the missing statistical comparisons.
open_obligations.partial_result: The deterministic part is completely settled by \(\mathrm{lem{:}deterministic\text{-}envelope\text{-}certificate}\): for continuous positive \(A,B\), the envelope has a unique minimizer and the convex-hull value has a certificate supported on at most two active parameter values.  Conditional on the uniform interior risk expansion and endpoint exclusion, balanced rounding changes \(m/\sqrt n\) by \(O(n^{-1/2})\); coercivity makes every asymptotically minimax pilot ratio precompact, and continuity plus uniqueness forces every subsequential limit to equal \(t^{\star}\).  The statistical premises of that conditional transfer remain open.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a balanced set \(T\), an action \(H\), and a unit \(i\in T\).  Let \(\mathcal G=\{-1,+1\}^{K_f}\) act on treatment labels by coordinatewise multiplication and on assignments by \((g z)_j=g z_j\).  This action preserves \(\Omega_T\), because it merely permutes the \(Q\) treatment cells.  The assumed flip invariance means
\[
p_{T,H}(g z)=p_{T,H}(z),\qquad g\in\mathcal G, z\in\Omega_T.
\]
For \(q\in\mathcal Q\), the definition of the exact inclusion probability and the bijective change of variable \(z=g u\) therefore give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{i,gq}(T,H)
&=\sum_{z\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(z)\mathbf 1\{z_i=gq\}\\
&=\sum_{u\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(g u)\mathbf 1\{g u_i=gq\}\\
&=\sum_{u\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(u)\mathbf 1\{u_i=q\}
=\pi_{iq}(T,H).
\end{aligned}
\]
The action of \(\mathcal G\) on \(\mathcal Q\) is transitive: for \(q,q'\in\mathcal Q\), choosing \(g=q'\odot q\) gives \(gq=q'\).  Hence \(\pi_{iq}(T,H)\) is constant in \(q\).  Since every assignment assigns unit \(i\) exactly one label, the definition of \(\pi_{iq}\) also yields
\[
\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\pi_{iq}(T,H)
=\sum_{z\in\Omega_T}p_{T,H}(z)
  \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}\mathbf 1\{z_i=q\}
=1.
\]
There are \(Q\) labels, so
\[
\pi_{iq}(T,H)=Q^{-1},\qquad i\in T, q\in\mathcal Q.
\]
In particular, the division in the Horvitz--Thompson formula is valid.  Define the observed treatment-cell mean
\[
\overline Y_T^{\mathrm{obs}}(q)
=\frac{Q}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T:Z_i=q}Y_{in}(q),
\]
which is well defined because balance gives exactly \(|T|/Q\) units in every cell.  Substitution of \(\pi_{iq}=Q^{-1}\) into the definition of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(H)\) gives, pointwise in the assignment,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_T(H)
&=\frac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i\in T}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}
 2^{1-K_f}c_q\,Q\mathbf 1\{Z_i=q\}Y_{in}(q)\\
&=2^{1-K_f}\sum_{q\in\mathcal Q}c_q\,
 \overline Y_T^{\mathrm{obs}}(q).
\end{aligned}
\]
The right-hand side is the ordinary balanced factorial difference-in-means estimator.

It remains to prove the two-wave assertion.  Take the action to be \(H=0\) in each wave.  Then every assignment in \(\Omega_T\) has score
\[
\Delta_T(z)^{\mathsf T}0\,\Delta_T(z)=0.
\]
Thus every assignment lies on the same boundary score.  By the common randomized boundary rule in the definition of \(a_{T,0}\), there is a constant \(c_T\) such that \(a_{T,0}(z)=c_T\) for every \(z\in\Omega_T\).  The exact-acceptance identity in \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}mixture}\) implies
\[
\alpha=|\Omega_T|^{-1}\sum_{z\in\Omega_T}a_{T,0}(z)=c_T.
\]
Substitution in the positive-support mixture, using \(\alpha>0\), gives
\[
p_{T,0}(z)=|\Omega_T|^{-1}
 \left\{\eta+(1-\eta)\frac{\alpha}{\alpha}\right\}
=|\Omega_T|^{-1}.
\]
Hence both wave assignments are conditionally uniform on their balanced supports; in particular their exact inclusion probabilities are \(Q^{-1}>0\).

Now let \(m\in\mathcal M_n\), put \(N=n-m\), and fix a full-sample balanced assignment \(z\in\Omega_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}\).  The definition of \(\mathcal M_n\), together with \(Q\mid n\), ensures that \(m/Q\), \(N/Q\), and \(n/Q\) are integers.  A pilot subset \(S\) is compatible with \(z\) precisely when it contains \(m/Q\) units from each of the \(Q\) treatment cells of \(z\).  Consequently the number of compatible subsets is
\[
L=\prod_{q\in\mathcal Q}{n/Q\choose m/Q}.
\]
For every set of the appropriate size,
\[
|\Omega_S|=\frac{m!}{(m/Q)!^Q},\qquad
|\Omega_{S^c}|=\frac{N!}{(N/Q)!^Q},\qquad
|\Omega_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}|=\frac{n!}{(n/Q)!^Q}.
\]
The pilot split is uniform, the pilot assignment is balanced complete randomization, and, conditionally on the pilot history, the zero-action main assignment is uniform by the calculation above.  The chain rule therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\{Z=z\}
&=\frac{L}{{n\choose m}|\Omega_S||\Omega_{S^c}|}\\
&=\frac{\{(n/Q)!/[(m/Q)!(N/Q)!]\}^Q}
{\{n!/(m!N!)\}\{m!/(m/Q)!^Q\}\{N!/(N/Q)!^Q\}}\\
&=\frac{(n/Q)!^Q}{n!}
=|\Omega_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}|^{-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This probability does not depend on \(z\), so the combined assignment is exactly uniform on the full-sample balanced support.

Finally, for every realized compatible triple \((S,Z_S,Z_{S^c})\), the zero-action inclusion probabilities are \(Q^{-1}\).  The pooled-estimator definition then gives the pointwise identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}_{n,m}(0)
&=\frac{m}{n}\frac{Q}{m}
  \sum_{i\in S}2^{1-K_f}c_{Z_i}Y_{in}(Z_i)
 +\frac{N}{n}\frac{Q}{N}
  \sum_{i\in S^c}2^{1-K_f}c_{Z_i}Y_{in}(Z_i)\\
&=\frac{Q}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n
 2^{1-K_f}c_{Z_i}Y_{in}(Z_i)
=\widehat{\boldsymbol\tau}^{\mathrm{HT}}_{T_n^{\mathrm{full}}}(0).
\end{aligned}
\]
The last quantity is the ordinary full-sample balanced factorial estimator by the first part.  Its exact-inclusion unbiasedness is also the corresponding special case of \(\mathrm{thm{:}exact\text{-}ht\text{-}accounting}\).  Every argument above is an exact finite-design identity.  No weak-convergence or covariance-limit premise was used, so the conclusion deliberately supplies no asymptotic limit law; such a law requires separate finite-population central-limit and covariance-limit conditions.
